The intersection of two Laguerre cells has zero Lebesgue measure
return as output the unique vector of optimal values for the Kantorovitch potentials $(w_1, \dots, w_N)$.
For $\alpha=0.75$, large deformations lead to more elongated and non-convex shapes (left).
Theorem~\ref{thm:semidiscrete} shows that for any such configuration, there is always a unique partition of the space that satisfies the volume constraint.

issues.failure_explanation: The stated hypotheses (each cost $c_i$ in $C^{1,1}(\Omega)$, nonnegative, with arbitrary seed positions) do not support the conclusions. (1) The potentials are never unique as stated: adding the same constant to all $w_i$ leaves every Laguerre cell unchanged, so 'uniquely defined' and the solver-output claim require a gauge. (2) Within the stated class the uniqueness claims fail: for two particles with identical cost functions (e.g. coincident seeds $x_1=x_2$ under the $L^2$ cost, with $0<v_1,v_2<1$) every volume-constrained partition has the same transport cost, so the Monge problem has no unique solution; if $w_1\neq w_2$ one cell is empty, while if $w_1=w_2$ the cells are not determined by the weights and two cells intersect in positive measure, contradicting both the volume condition and the zero-measure-intersection claim. The cited references establish such results only under additional non-degeneracy (twist-type) assumptions not stated here. (3) Conversely, the paper's own cost families -- power costs $|y-x|^\alpha$ with $\alpha<2$ (used with $\alpha=0.5,0.75,1$) and polar costs $(|x-x_i|/r_0(\theta))^p$ with $p<2$ -- are not $C^{1,1}$ at the seed point, so the theorem as stated does not even apply to the paper's central soft-particle experiments.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the theorem with explicit non-degeneracy hypotheses (distinct seeds/costs and a twist-type condition, as in the cited references), qualify uniqueness of the Kantorovich potentials 'up to an additive constant' (fixed by the solver's anchoring), and adjust or extend the smoothness assumption so that costs which are continuous with twist away from the seed -- in particular the power costs with $\alpha<2$ used throughout the paper -- are covered.
issues.overall_effect: The foundational guarantee that the optimal transport solver returns a unique, well-defined partition (the cell shapes) with the prescribed volumes for any configuration -- restated as 'for any such configuration, there is always a unique partition' -- is not established as stated: degenerate configurations break uniqueness and well-definedness of the cells, the potentials are only unique up to an additive constant, and the soft-particle regime ($\alpha<2$) lies outside the stated hypotheses.
issues.title: Semi-discrete transport theorem asserts uniqueness under insufficient and mismatched cost hypotheses
issues.why_classification: moderate_issue: the repair goes beyond fixing a degenerate case (gauge qualification, non-degeneracy hypotheses, and coverage of the paper's own non-$C^{1,1}$ costs), but a contained restatement/extension preserves the method, all experiments and the advertised scope; no substantive result or regime must be abandoned.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The shape $\mathscr{S}\subset\Omega$ that minimizes the individual energy
Then let $\mathscr{S}\subset\Omega$ be any shape of volume $v_i$.

issues.failure_explanation: The statement minimizes over all shapes with no volume constraint -- since $c\ge 0$ the minimizer would then be the empty set -- and the proof silently restricts to shapes of volume $v_i$. Even with that constraint, the key step is an invalid inference: monotonicity of $U$ together with $U(0)=0$ and $U\to1$ yields a $w^*$ with $U(w^*)=v_i$ only if $U$ is continuous, and a unique one only if $U$ is strictly increasing; neither is established. $U(0)=|\{c=0\}|$ need not be $0$, and $U$ can jump: a $C^{1,1}$ nonnegative cost that is constant on a set of positive measure at a non-extremal level (e.g. on an annulus) makes $U$ skip values; for such $v_i$ no level set has volume $v_i$, and the true minimizers (a sublevel set plus part of the flat level set, or subsets of a positive-measure zero-cost set) are not of the form $\{c\le w\}$. The exchange argument itself is valid once a suitable $w^*$ exists.

failure_location.quote: First of all, since the function $U : w \mapsto |\mathscr{S}(w)|$ is non-decreasing, $U(0)=0$ and $U(w)\to1$ as $w\to+\infty$ there exists a unique $w^*>0$ such that $U(w^*) = v_i$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the volume constraint $|\mathscr{S}|=v_i$ to the statement and assume that the cost's zero set and level sets have zero Lebesgue measure (so that $U$ is continuous and strictly increasing); this holds for the radially increasing costs used in the paper, and the proof then goes through unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The level-set characterization of preferred shapes -- used to claim that any particle shape can be realized by a suitable cost and that the correct level set is automatically selected by the Kantorovich potential -- is established only under implicit extra hypotheses (null zero-cost set, no positive-measure flat level sets).
issues.title: Preferred-shape lemma: existence and uniqueness of the sublevel parameter is an invalid inference, and the statement omits the volume constraint
issues.why_classification: minor_issue: a short, local repair (add the omitted constraint and a standard null-level-set condition satisfied by every cost used in the paper) preserves the lemma and all its downstream uses, with no new lemma or replacement argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: which corresponds to lowering the potential and thus allowing deformations in the directions of large nonnegative gradients. This produces elongated shapes
Since the morphological changes are biased in the direction of increasing gradient, this choice induces chemotactic migration.
This corresponds to a larger cost in the direction of larger gradient but even larger for negative gradient. This produces fan-like shapes

issues.failure_explanation: By the paper's own Lemma \ref{lemma:prefferedshape} (and the Laguerre cell versus the zero-cost medium), a particle's shape is the sublevel set $\{c\le w\}$ of its cost; since $\varphi=-\log c$ (so $c=e^{-\varphi}$), the shape is a superlevel set of $\varphi$, and lowering $\varphi$ in a direction raises the cost there and retracts the shape. The perturbations enter as $\varphi=\varphi_0+\beta f$: with $f(\delta)=-\delta_+$ the potential is lowered exactly in directions of positive chemo-attractant gradient, so the cell retracts from the attractant, deforms away from it, and the barycenter-driven migration points away from the attractant (anti-chemotaxis), contradicting 'allowing deformations in the directions of large nonnegative gradients', the claimed elongated shapes toward the gradient, and 'induces chemotactic migration'. Likewise $f=\delta_-^2+\delta_+$ lowers the cost (rather than raising it, pace 'a larger cost in the direction of larger gradient') and yields along-gradient elongation rather than a fan orthogonal to the gradient; and the protrusion perturbation $f=-\sum_k\xi_kG_{\theta_k}\le 0$ produces local cost increases (dents), not protrusions. The described phenomenology is consistent only with the opposite sign convention (e.g. $\varphi=\log c$, or negating $f$).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Flip the sign convention: define $\varphi=\log c$ (equivalently, negate the perturbations $f$ in Eqs. \ref{eq:perturblong}-\ref{eq:perturbfan} and in the protrusion model), so that lowering the potential lowers the cost and extends the shape; all claimed behaviours then follow and the accompanying verbal justifications become correct.
issues.overall_effect: As specified, the chemotaxis model (Eqs. \ref{eq:perturblong} and \ref{eq:perturbfan}) and the random-protrusion model of Section \ref{sec:random_cost} produce deformations and centroid migration opposite to those described in the text, figure captions and video descriptions; they fail their stated purpose (chemotactic migration, protrusion-driven random exploration).
issues.title: Sign inversion in the biased-cost models: chemotaxis and protrusion constructions act opposite to the claimed behavior
issues.why_classification: minor_issue: the repair is a local sign correction of the potential's definition applied consistently to both models; it requires no new construction or argument and preserves every claimed behaviour (indeed restores it).
